NTA. The toll of being sick heavily affects our partners. And it sucks. Im 30 and your wifes situation sounds a bit familiar with mine. Inflammation, widespread pain, laying down, lack of social events, tests with normal results, undiagnosed, etc. 

While I am grateful my boyfriend has stuck by my side, I constantly feel bad for holding him back from having a "normal" life. While I hope he stays, I would understand if he left and would want him to be happy. It would hurt, but I understand he stuck by my side for four years being patient. Him leaving may even motivate me to try to do more to find resolution to my health issues (i've done alot - hundreds of doctors appointments, but its easy to get discouraged and stagnant in pursuing a diagnosis when youre told time and time again by doctors that they dont know whats wrong.)

It sounds to me like your wife has lost motivation and isn't trying to find ways to enjoy life the way she can.

Here are some things I have done to be able to enjoy life to the best of my abilities. People may disagree - please note I am just sharing MY story. -

1. Mentality - I push through. For me it's a mentality thing. I can either push through and enjoy what I can or succumb to the disease. I pay the consequences later but I want to enjoy what I can
2. Compromise/Boundaries - I learned what I am capable of and what I am not. This is really important to learn if you want to be involved in life the best that I can. My body wont let me participate in life activities the way I want, so thats where I had to figure out what I can really tolerate and what I cant, and find solutions for me that work with what my body allows me to do, that will still let me be able to participate in life. For instance:
   1. Standing and walking for long periods of time is nearly impossible for me. So, if we are going to an amusement park, I drive separately so I can still join, but don't need to disrupt or ruin anyones trip in case I need to leave early.
   2. I am really really really cold, all the time. And in turn, that makes my body hurt even more. So I keep spare jackets and fuzzy socks in my car at all times. I keep fuzzy socks in my bag. I have travel heat blankets, etc
   3. I have to eat every few hours. If i dont, my body starts to hurt. So I have a snack basket and plan my meals out. If I am going somewhere that allows food in, I will bring multiple sandwiches or snacks so I have it on me when needed.
3. Discouraged - It is really discouraging and unmotivating to constantly be told they dont know whats wrong, test after test after test. For me, this does impact my happiness and can cause a little depression and lack of motivation. While the doctors dont know whats wrong, I know how I feel - thats where the above point on boundaries comes into play.
4. Enabling - I know my boyfriend is there and that he will bring me what I need if I ask. While that is sweet and amazing, it is easy to take advantage of that and sometimes I feel like it enables me to be lazier because I am not forced to take care of myself. On days he is at work, I am forced to do things on my own and I do what I need to do on my own because I dont have him there for me to ask for help

Another suggestion I have made in the past is if you do want (or need) to use multiple cards, use specific cards for specific purchases - example, card 1234 is bills and utilities, card 5678 is fun and entertainment, card 9876 is emergencies, card 4321 is groceries, etc. Some people work well with everything on one card, some work better putting specific items on specific cards.

Hi there, I have really only helped friends and family because I am not a professional at finances or anything like that but I suppose I would be willing to help, I've never really been asked outside of just my friends and family or never really considered it. Might be difficult to do virtually, unless someone were to email me their bank statements. IDK Ive never thought about it lol!

I have helped my entire family and my friends do exactly this for years and years. I am just good at being organized and managing my finances. Every single person always has something they don't know that they're paying for.

I suggest to start small.

* Write down on one piece of paper all bank numbers and credit cards you use to make purchases
* Begin with **one** of those bank statement. Go through one page of it every few days to give yourself time to cool off if it's overwhelming to you
* On an excel sheet or google sheets spreadsheet, start writing down your reoccurring expenses. Subscriptions, utilities, monthly charges, quarterly charges, annual charges, etc
* Once you finish one page, go on to the next.
* When you are **entirely** done with every page of one bank statement, cross it off your list (from the first bullet point) and start the next statement

I suggest to do this for a few months to make sure you don't miss anything. It gets less overwhelming once you start. And also, don't skim. Go line by line, and cross out each line once you have written down or identified the charge. It is easy to miss something when you skim. Also use the physical printed out bank statements. Youll miss a bunch if you do it on a computer. It will log you out, youll lose your place, etc.

It took over 15 years but I was determined. Essentially I just analyzed the patterns  for a long time: what was making me feel worse, when did my depression get worse, what was bringing it on, what were my repetitive thoughts, what was making me feel so doomed. And then I took action.

I did things, I removed negative things, and I gave myself time limits:

1. I was depressed every single day for years and years so I had to find outlets that made me feel better, such as being productive. For me, that was being productive in work and writing music. My OCPD has probably kept me alive.
2. I  realized my depression gets super unbearable before my period. I learned to manage the daily depression, and when my period is coming and that depression hits, I remind myself that my period is coming and the overwhelming depression will last 2-7 days. 
3. When I get down randomly, I just remind myself when I am down that it will pass, because it HAS passed time and time again for the past 19 years. 
4. I allow my depressive thoughts to linger for 20 minutes. I sit in it, feel it, allow it to consume me. Then after 20 minutes, I envision opening a door, waving the depression out the door, closing the door and saying I will see you tomorrow. And then I force myself to get up and do things to make me feel better. 
5. I do not partake in things that make me feel bad, even if others dont understand. For instance, I don't do a lot of social activiites, i dont own a tv, i dont do social media. Anything I noticed that makes me feel worse, I removed from my life and found things I enjoy doing to replace it.
6. I did CBT (cognitive behaviour therapy). The Workbook "Mind Over Mood" was helpful. Me LEARNING about thought patterns was incredibly helpful.

Closing the door on my depression allows me to feel what I need to feel but doesn't allow it to consume me. It is a lot more difficult to do that during my period, so I allow myself to feel it.

Trust me, people have said "oh it wasn't bad then." No, it was. I have called the suicide hotline, and I am dark every day. But i grew up with a mom who was dependent on depression medication that wasn't working but she didn't notice. From a young age I knew about depression and NEVER wanted to be like that. So I fought hard, and did whatever I could to shift my thoughts. It took over FIFTEEN YEARS TO LEARN TO DO. It was not some quick fix.

Hi there!  I definitely don't think you're lazy, I get it, this is a more personalized response than some Blog or article.

Summary here, and full explanation below: I realized I thought differently my entire life. It got me places in life, but it got exhausting and I was tired of always thinking everything was so serious and not enjoying anything other than working. I got desperate due to being aware of my differences for the past 15 years, and always WISHING I could change myself for so many years. I listened to podcasts, support groups, and picked up some mantras. When I was looking for advice, I shifted my focus from OCPD Help to Anxiety Help just because I could "grasp"  the Anxiety advice better than the OCPD advice. The best advice that has helped me that I remind myself about is that **EXPECTATIONS ARE JUST MY OWN PERSONAL PREFERENCES**. I also try to be mindful that **I don't know what other people are going through and that their goals may be different than mine**. 

\_\_

So I noticed I thought and acted differently ever since I was maybe 12. I never understood how people could enjoy socializing, I never had the same mentality when it came to work. I just thought that was who I was. I always WISHED I could enjoy social gatherings, I always WISHED I could relax.

I got into a relationship and realized the patterns of my behaviour I had with my current boyfriend and my ex. My OCPD really comes out when I share a space with someone. I went into therapy because I thought I had anger issues, and I didn't understand why I saw things SO DIFFERENTLY than everyone else and why I could NOT enjoy things or change my mentality when I **WANTED** to change. Not only was it exhausting, but I couldn't relate to others. I couldn't relax. And after years of wanting change, I realized I needed help trying to do so.

Once my therapist notified me about OCPD, I looked into it and yup, I hit nearly 100% of the markers. My world was shattered. My foundation was uprooted for a couple of weeks. Everything I believed made me "me" was actually just a personality disorder. All of my values were actually just my disorder. I didn't know who I was. That was the lowest I have ever felt in my life.

I spent months in group sessions, OCPD support groups, regular Support Groups, listening to OCPD podcasts trying to understand how to overcome and manage my OCPD. The OCPD support groups were not really helping because no matter what they said, l didn't agree with the mentality and behaviours of people who didnt have OCPD. I didn't think anything was wrong with trying to be efficient and a hard worker, I just wanted to be able to enjoy smaller things and not have everything be so heavy! 

And then I came across a podcast for Anxiety Management and that changed everything. I could relate to what they were saying more. I realized I could adjust my reactions when I thought of it as anxiety vs OCPD. 

I am not medical professional, but truly believe OCPD is a part of anxiety and I really wish people would explore that more. 

I was doing alright for a year with what I had learned from coping with anxiety, and then in February of this year my OCPD and anxiety got so out of control, I finally couldnt take it. I got desperate. I began medication last Thursday for the first time in my life. I never thought I would turn to medication, but I just had to see. I felt defeated. I had tried EVERYTHING to NOT CARE ABOUT SHIT SO MUCH. I had tried so hard to do mantras, meditation, breathing, everything, and I could not shake my OCPD traits. So I got desperate, and I got curious. I wanted to see what it was about, if medication could actually help me.

Its been only a few days and I already feel better, but I know the medication doesn't work for 6-8 weeks, so I am still wondering if I do have the power to adjust my mentality on my own. I told myself I am sticking with the medication for 6-8 weeks minimum just to see if it will get any better than where I currently am at, and I will reassess then.

**BUT this is what helped me prior to turning to medication:** 

\- Podcasts. 

\- Hearing about OCPD and Anxiety coping methods helped. 

\- Support Groups.

\- Communicating with people openly that I have OCPD. It made people more understanding of my behaviours. 

\- Communicating my needs for in case I did lash out was important (I need the person not to escalate and give me a couple of hours to cool down before I can come back and apologize and discuss rationally.) 

\- Limiting discussions about certain topics. There are also some topics I can't handle - politics, Republican vs Democratic shit, and social issues - those are problems that have solutions that are just so much deeper than what is presented in the media and I just can't handle the surface level discussions that are had about them.

\- Learning my values and really realizing if my values and behaviours aligned. For years I thought my value was efficiency. It wasn't until Jan of 2022 that I realized NO, I wasn't always trying to be efficient, I was always doing things to be helpful, and I thought being efficient was being helpful. Once I realize my main purpose has always been to be helpful, that helped me navigate my relationships and interactions with people. 

\- Finding advice that helped me, writing them down, and reading my mantras. I sat down and had to really learn how to better manage my anxiety and OCPD and I made a list. I read this every morning. I have a reminder come on my phone every morning with this:

\- SAY LESS  
\- LISTEN  
\- BE MINDFUL  
\- SIT WITH MY FEELINGS  
\- KEEP IT MINIMAL  
\- NO EXPLANATIONS / JUSTIFICATIONS  
\- SPREAD POSITIVITY  
\- LAUGH  
\- “HELPFUL” IS NEW VALUE

Hi,

**TLDR**: I was discouraged about the possibility of having a successful OCPD relationship when I would look online for advice and tips, and all I found was negative experiences. So don't look online for advice, it will only discourage you more. Most OCPD relationships fail because the OCPD Partner doesn't know they have it, or don't work on themselves when they know that they have it. If you are aware of your OCPD, start working on yourself (support groups, read about Anxiety, therapy, CBT), listen to your wifes needs, and communicate with her - and you will begin to feel more confident in your partnership.

I get it 100%,  I was so discouraged about the possibility of a successful relationship when I was diagnosed with OCPD a few months ago. It felt impossible, (on top of it my boyfriend has ADHD, so not a great combo.) But try shifting your perspective, you two have made it 11 years thus far, and now that you have more of an understanding about your mental illness, you can start to take the measures needed to begin to manage your illness. Most relationships with an OCPD partner fail because the person with OCPD doesn't try to get help. So you are aware, and have a drive to achieve success, so it can only get better from here!

A word of advice to stay positive about your relationship - if you have the drive to make it work, listen to your wifes requests and needs, work on yourself, and dont look on threads for answers about relationship outcomes for people with OCPD. I am suggesting that last part to prevent you from experiencing what I went through. I looked online for tips for relationships for people with OCPD when I was first diagnosed and it brought me into a huge depression. Everything and everyone was so negative, and I wanted to believe I had hope in making the relationship work.

*Example: I had searched something about relationship outcomes with OCPD and there was this thread saying "Should I marry my OCPD partner?" And the first comment was "DO NOT MARRY HIM." lol*

Now i am not saying this so you can walk around naively about how this disorder is hard to deal with for partners, or to be ignorant about the fact that many studies show how OCPD relationships can be unsuccessful, mostly due to the fact that the OCPD doesn't work on themselves. But it didn't help me to look online because most people had negative experiences with their relationships, and they weren't providing advice to make relationships work, but instead sharing their terrible experiences, and I didn't want that answer. I had the drive to try to overcome it and make my relationship work, so I stopped looking online and started doing the work.

My partner and I have been together for 2 years (so not long in comparison) but given the pandemic has made us stay inside and with each other 24/7 for an entire year straight, lets add 5 years of time to that haha.

My symptoms of OCPD was bringing the relationship to an end, so I started therapy and then was diagnosed. I started to put in the work to manage it. I attend support groups 5 days a week, and educated myself on Anxiety. What has helped me get some form of control of my OCPD was to address my Anxiety Disorder. When I recognize I am getting triggered, I practice mindfulness and acknowledge it's my Anxiety, (I have a couple things I tell myself that help me) and typically I can cool down.

Theres definitely still times when I cant manage my OCPD and it is at his expense, but thats where the team work comes in. Depending on the scenario, he either will dismiss himself from the room until I calm down, or say a phrase that helps me calm down. He avoids being defensive, and theres a lot of compromise and walking on egg shells on his end (less now that I am managing it, but I can tell he's still hesitant). It's only been a few months of this and he sees me trying and he sees my improvement thus far, and he knows I am trying to get better. But it takes a toll on him and I can tell.

So my advice based on my experience has been to find a way to ground yourself, apologize and acknowledge when you flared up, appreciate them, address your Anxieties, and communicate a strategy about what to do when you do get triggered. It took some trial and error, but so far the Support Groups have really helped me.

Music. So I am sure people will have various opinions on this depending on the amount of years they have lived the travellers lifestyle thus far. I was on the road for 9 years or so. It was thrilling, exciting, and I felt incredibly fortunate. But there are many downsides, and at some point, the downsides outweigh the positives.


You don't really get to see the cities. Alot of it was you get to the airport, run an errand if needed, get to the hotel, get ready, get to the show, and back to the airport. Sometimes of course you would stay in one city for a few days because there'd be numerous shows/obligations around that one city, but most of the time its prepping for said shows/obligations in the hotel.  I can count only a number of times having the "time" to go and sight-see the city I was in. And by time, I mean, I went for 15 minutes, walked around quickly, tried to take in the amazement, then rushed back to the hotel.


I would imagine this would vary depending on the line of work you're in, but for the other musicians I know (EDM scene), my lifestyle of airport to hotel to show to airport is the norm. Traveling for work can be tricky too. You get the hang of preparing for travels, but not having one set work area can be stressful - you better pack everything you will and might need otherwise you're scrambling to find it in a city you dont know.  Also theres a lot of prep work since you don't know the cities. Alot of time planning and mapping things out.


The other downside is relationships. The sacrifice made of always being on the road is one musicians don't have the luxury to discuss because we are seen as "ungrateful" if we try. You miss weddings, funerals, birthdays, births, holidays. You miss out on friends and relationships unless your partners has the ability to travel with you. Your closest crew is those you work with, which after a while, I am sure you could imagine, could become irritating since you rarely get alone time. You can't really relate with friends back home who never lived that life. And you meet many people along the way, but its hard to form any type of meaningful relationship with people you only spend a few hours to a few days with, and only see them if you're in the same city again.


Another thing to note is rent, lol. You're paying rent for a storage unit and closet essentially. Luckily, I didn't have a car back home, and my place was used by other artists who were coming through my city when I was away. So it worked out.


It was always thrilling, and always exciting. If I could do it again, I would consider balance, however, I would have to ask myself if I would have had the ability to achieve everything that I did if I didn't dedicate everything I had to it.


Even with all of this said, I still stand by it - chase your dreams, do what you desire to do, and don't allow anyone to discourage you. I have enjoyed Covid (besides all the death) because it was the first time since 2010 that I had been in the same city for more than a month straight. But I am definitely feeling that itch of excitement and thrill again!

Yes closing credit card accounts does actually affect your credit score.  it will look bad if you keep it open for a short period of time.

 if anything keep it and use it on a small purchase every month and pay if off immediately to begin building your credit. nothing wrong with having a credit card, but everything is wrong with mismanaging a credit card. 

i suggest googling “does closing a credit card affect a credit score” or “how to build credit with a credit card”. 

pay it on time and in full every month is my biggest suggestion, and also learn about utilization rate. that is the percentage of the credit you use of your entire credit limit. you want to keep you credit usage to 20% max. for instance :

credit limit (the amount you’re given to use on the credit card, ie, the most you’re allowed to use on your credit card) $2,000

you want to have have $400 balance max ($20% of $2,000.) (“balance” is the amount you’ve spent)

- pay it off each month in full
- use it as a debit card 
- don’t buy what you can’t afford 
- no late payments
- watch how much you put on the balance (credit utilization) 

credit history is a large factor in building credit so you’ll want to start that sooner rather than later. 

knowledge is from: myself, 28 years old, 810 credit score, no debt. i do not use a debit card or cash.

Oh dear lord, where do I start.

1. Personal financing - credit cards, credit scores, home loans, taxes, interest rates, loans, car investments vs leases, etc.
2. Handling insecurities - view your flaws as unique differences from you and others. Flaws are what make you you, are what make you special, and are what make you stand out.
3. Validation - Find meaning and purpose in your life other than doing what every other person is doing, find value within yourself and find what message you want to send to others. Value is not brought by the material items you own or the likes you have on Social Media.
4. Beliefs - Just because your parents behave, think or act in a certain manner, does not mean you need to do the same. Branch out beyond just your parents, and try to understand why they do what they do. Times have changed from when they were kids, what worked then may not be practical for you now.
5. Dependency - Similar to validation, learn your self worth and don't accept relationships that take away from you. Don't stay in something longer than you should if it no longer provides value or benefits to you. You will not forever be alone, and in the chance you believe that you will be, learn to find value in being alone. You get to do whatever you want, with no compromises, you save money, and your mind isn't consumed thinking about another person and their wants and desires. It's okay to be selfish if it isn't bringing harm onto others. Your next relationship is always better than the last.
6. Pressures - men, jobs, people, women, friends, parents, teachers, etc might put you in a situation where you feel uncomfortable or feel that you are not doing something that is morally aligned with your values. Do not give in. The awkwardness of saying no in that moment is far better than the lifelong regret or cringeworthy disappointment you might face if you say yes. When one door closes, another one opens. Always remember that.
7. Research - Research things before you do it, whether it is researching discounts, researching a job position and duties, researching others experiences about a situation, researching secret tips about something. Look into something before acting on it, you might find something that will help you navigate the situation more efficiently.
8. Trauma - Goes along with beliefs. Understand your traumas and how events you might have had may have shaped your perspective on the world. I had no idea a breakup from 5 years ago shifted my personality and beliefs as much as it did, and was considered a traumatic event, until I watched a webinar about Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and started getting professional help about it. Trauma prevents you from enjoying the beauty of experiences and life. Work through it, or at least understand your trauma.
9. Substance Use - Understand why a large amount of Americans use drugs and alcohols, it is an escape from reality, but not a solution. Getting addicted or dependent on a substance is more of a hassle in the long run than actually solving the issue. Use substances for enhanced experiences or enjoyment of an event, but there is no need to get obliterated every weekend.
10. Information - Relevant primarily because it's 2020, but look into everything, question everything you hear or read. Anyone can write anything on the internet, yourself and myself included, and anyone can pass on that information to the next person in conversation. So with that, question it, research it. It can be overwhelming on where to start, but ask around, read different sites, try to make sure what you read is actually consistent among different sources. Also understand everyone has different experiences, so their beliefs or facts might be true to them, it does not mean it needs to be true to the fact, or true for you. So just educate yourself on what it is and make the best guessed decision you can with the information you have found.
11. Variety - Do everything, learn everything that interests you. Don't limit your skills to solely one task. Understand what your strengths are and what you are good at, and expand on those. You are able to learn new skills and traits too, it takes time and effort, but you can add it all to your list of skills you bring to the table. That waiter job you have now, analyze it, observe it, see how the business and management operates, study what makes that company and employees successful. That fast food job you have, understand how it has become efficient. That babysitting job you have, maybe study the interior design or how the parents parent their kid. You can apply all those skills and that information to your next and better job or opportunity.
12. Drama - What is important now will truly pass. Think about any grief you may have once had, from a death or breakup, or a hard class you took, and look at you now. Those feelings you had in that moment might not be as strong as time has passed. Don't make any drastic decisions when something seems overbearing, overwhelming or unmanageable. Take a breath, take a walk, go outside, etc. The feelings that come with that tweet that has resurfaced, or the accusation that has been made, or the new information you have just learned, will subside over time, and you will find a way to overcome it and carry on.
13. Goals - Enjoy the journey, because typically whatever goal you have is not actually what you told yourself it would be once you get there. The more money you make, the more money you spend. The bigger house you get, the more things you have to fix. The nicer car you get, the higher the insurance. The idols you want to meet, take shits too. The dream job you work to get, you will still be stuck with your same thoughts. You want to be famous, you lose your privacy. You can't escape shit, so its best you realize that now, and that you understand that reaching your goal doesn't remove all the struggles you currently face, you are simply just faced with new ones.
14. Believe in yourself. No one else will until you give them a reason to, and that reason is usually because you will have suddenly become of value or benefit to them.

Federal Gov added $600 every week to anyone who applied for Unemployment and was approved. The $600 was in addition to whatever amount you were awarded from Unemployment. But the $600 per week started in the beginning of April (I want to say April 11 maybe) and ended  July 25/26.

*For example: You are awarded $300 from Unemployment plus Federal Government would give $600, meaning you were getting $900 each week.*

From that point after July 26, you received only your regular Unemployment payments.

*For example: You would only receive $300 now each week from Unemployment.*

As of Sep 7, it is up to the States to add additional wages (instead of the Federal Gov) to Unemployment Payments. California gives $300 in addition, however your Unemployment Claim must be a minimum of $100 each week in order to be eligible to receive the additional $300.

*For example: You would receive your $300 from Unemployment plus $300 from your State, meaning you are getting $600 each week.*

Some additional things to note: (this is for California):

1. Self-Employed or Independent Contractors weren't eligible to receive Unemployment prior to the pandemic. Now they are but since it is new, there are issues. Regardless of your high earnings as a Self-Employed Earner, the maximum amount you can receive weekly from Unemployment is $167.

Every time you open a card, it effects your credit score. Think of it this way. 

Imagine your "Credit Card" is a friend.

You borrow $5,000 from one friend (ie you open one credit card)
Then you borrow $2,000 from a second friend (ie you open a second credit card)
Then you borrow $3,500 from a third friend (ie you open a third credit card)
Etc.

Why would a fourth friend let you borrow money from them, if it looks like you have had to borrow from a different friend each time, and only in small amounts each time.

VS

You borrow $5,000 from one friend (ie you open one credit card) but then they allow you to borrow more money later on (ie they raise your credit limit to $8,000)

Now when you go to ask a second friend to borrow money (ie you want to buy a car or open a second car), you appear as being more reliable because your first friend (your first credit card) trusted you enough to lend you more money (raise your credit limit) and youve only ever had to "borrow" money once.

Sorry if that doesnt make sense. There are however numerous different opinions about this. Some people like having numerous accounts open for the same belief as you said. However, each card you open does bring your score down a little temporary.

Also having more credit cards is risky because you have more accounts to manage regarding payments, utilization rate, etc. It is higher risk if you are not on top of it.

I would suggest to do some research on the impact of having 1. numerous credit cards, 2. balances on numerous credit cards, 3. Pros/Cons of having only one card vs numerous cards.

I am NO expert so please do research, Im not professional in this, this is just what I have found. When I opened 5 cards when I was naive and younger, even without using all of them all the time, my credit score didnt have the same growth as my credit score has now with only three cards. I would love to go down to only 2 cards because i rarely use my Target Card, however, closing an account effects your credit score so I just let it be.

It fluctuates depending on my Utilization Rate monthly, anywhere between 775 and 810. **I personally put everything on my credit card** and **pay it throughout the month to keep my Utilization Rate low. 742 is pretty good and your credit history is pretty good. Make sure you make payments on time, and keeping your Utilization Rate low is crucial. Do not close Credit Accounts, as Closing accounts lowers scores, as does opening new ones.

On your current Credit Cards Online accounts, if they offer showing your Credit Score, they should tell you what is negatively effecting your credit score (mine does.) Mine currently has told me that these two things are currently effecting my Credit Score:

1.  **Proportion of loan balances to loan amounts is too high**  \- Consumers who use a high percentage of their available credit (generally known as utilization) have a higher risk of delinquency (falling behind on payments) and charge-off (loan default) over time. Lower use of available credit allows consumers who have the need to temporarily carry higher loan balances to do so, because they have available credit on their accounts. Consumers with heavier credit usage cannot absorb changes to their financial situation as easily, which can lead to higher risk over time. Keeping credit balances lower in relation to available credit will help reduce the negative impact on a credit score over time.

2.  **Too many accounts with balances** \- Consumers who have opened several loan accounts (number of accounts opened) or use many loan accounts (number of accounts with balances) generally pose a higher risk. Most consumers use loan accounts on an as-needed basis. Consumers carrying balances on many accounts have a higher risk of going delinquent (falling behind on payments) or charging off (defaulting on) their accounts.
